objective.statement: Understand root-position chords with any spacing and doubling.
successCriteria: I know a chord may use its notes more than once, at any octave.
I know a chord is in root position when its root is the lowest note.
I can name a chord however its notes are spaced.

explanation.text: A chord is three or more notes played together. The simplest chord is just a triad, but a chord may use the notes of a triad more than once, at any octave, and the notes are usually spaced out with gaps between them. Here are three chords made from the tonic triad of C major.

music.textAlternative: Three bars of 4/4, each with a C major chord: C, E, G close together; the same notes with C doubled at the top; then C, G and E spread out.

explanation.caption: Three chords of C major: close, with the root doubled, and spread out.

explanation.text: The lowest note of each chord is the root, C, so all are 'in root position'. That is the only thing you need to know to name them: find the lowest note, say which degree of the scale it is, and the degree tells you the chord. Doubling a note or spacing the notes differently does not change the chord.

If a different note of the triad is at the bottom, the chord is not in root position (it is an inversion, which you will meet in Grade 5). At Grade 4, chords you are asked to name are always in root position, but you may be asked how you can tell: the root, the note the triad is built on, is the lowest sounding note.
Root position: the root is the lowest note. Spacing and doubling never change the chord. Name a chord by its lowest note.

music.textAlternative: One bar of 4/4 with a bass-clef chord: F, C, A, F.

steps: The lowest note is F: the root.
The notes are F, C, A and F: F twice, so the root is doubled.
F is the 4th degree of C major: chord IV.
demonstration.textAlternative: A spread chord on F in C major: chord IV.

parts.prompt: Is the chord in root position?

options.label: Yes: the root is the lowest note
No: the lowest note is not the root

yes.reason: The lowest note is not the root here. Arrange the three different notes in a stack of 3rds: the bottom of that stack is the root.

parts.prompt: Which note is the root of the chord?

A.reason: A is the 3rd of the chord, not the root. Stack the notes in 3rds from the bottom.

C.reason: C is the lowest note, but the root is the bottom note of the stack of 3rds, not necessarily the lowest note you can hear.

hints: The root is the bottom of the stack of thirds.
The root is the note you can build the others on by adding thirds: root, 3rd, 5th. The lowest note is the root only in root position.

feedback.correct: Yes: the root is the bottom note of the stack of 3rds.

mistakes.concept-misapplied: You found the right place, but check the rule you used — see the hint for that part.

provenance.notes: Original wording. Follows Grade 4 outcome 15 and First Steps Grade 4 section 11 (pp. 95-96): chords vs triads, repeated notes, spacing, root position as the lowest note.
